title: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction https://www.teachertoolkit.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Principles-of-Insruction-Rosenshine.pdf
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), November 15, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton's page distills Barak Rosenshine's classic 'Principles of Instruction,' which draws ten research-based teaching principles from cognitive science, studies of master teachers, and research on cognitive supports. The principles run from daily review and presenting material in small steps through to frequent questioning, modeling, guided practice, and weekly or monthly review, forming a coherent sequence rather than a checklist of unrelated tips. Rosenshine emphasizes that working memory is the binding constraint on learning, so effective teachers break content into small chunks, secure a high success rate during practice, and only fade support as students demonstrate mastery. The paper also stresses that checking for understanding is not a courtesy but a diagnostic act, since it is how teachers catch misconceptions before they harden into long-term errors. Barton highlights that these principles are complementary across their three source disciplines, which is part of why they have proven so durable in professional development circles.
points: Aim for roughly an 80% success rate during guided and independent practice — high enough to signal real learning is happening, not so high that students aren't being appropriately challenged.
Daily review is not filler: it strengthens prior learning, improves fluent recall, and was central to a successful elementary maths intervention Rosenshine cites.
Scaffolds like checklists, cue cards, and modeled thinking-aloud should be withdrawn gradually as competence grows, not removed all at once or left in place indefinitely.
Choral responses can boost participation in vocabulary or list-based practice, but only work if the teacher ensures every student starts answering together.
quotes: This research paper presents ten research-based principles of effective instruction.
Begin each lesson with a short review of material covered previously. This can strengthen prior learning and lead to more fluent recall.
Present new material in small steps with student practice after each step. Students' working memory has a limited capacity.
Ask a large number of questions and check the responses of all students. Questions provide practice and help students connect new material to prior learning.
Obtain a high success rate. Aiming for a success rate of around 80% during instruction and practice activities indicates that students are learning the material while being challenged.
Engage students in weekly and monthly review. Regular review is essential for students to develop a well-connected and readily accessible body of knowledge.
The most effective teachers ensured that students efficiently acquired, rehearsed, and connected knowledge.
